name: Container orchestration
summary: Software that keeps your containers running, wherever there’s room.
howItWorks: An orchestrator runs containers across a fleet of machines. You declare the desired state (three copies of `api:1.4.2`, 512 MB each) and a control loop keeps making reality match it. It places containers on machines with free capacity, restarts crashed ones, replaces them when a machine dies, rolls out new versions gradually and gives each group a stable address.
analogy: An air-traffic controller for containers. You file the flight plan; it picks the runway, and it reroutes when one closes.
useWhen: Dozens of services that need scheduling, discovery and rolling deploys
Self-healing: failed containers come back without a human
One consistent platform across clouds or on-prem
avoidWhen: One or two services: a managed container runner like Cloud Run or Fargate is far less to operate
Teams without time to learn, upgrade and secure the cluster itself
Learning or testing on one machine: a local cluster from kind or minikube is enough
example: An API runs as a Kubernetes Deployment with 3 replicas. At 2 a.m. a node fails. The scheduler sees only 2 pods running, starts a replacement on a healthy node, and nobody gets paged.

providers.aws: EKS, ECS; Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA)
providers.oss: Kubernetes and Nomad. Kubernetes distributions: K3s, RKE2, MicroK8s, Talos Linux, OKD, and Red Hat OpenShift (commercial); Rancher manages many clusters; kubeadm bootstraps your own; kind and minikube run a cluster on a laptop

diagram.caption: The Service spreads requests across three pods. When node-2 disappears, traffic skips it and the control plane starts a replacement, because the desired count is still 3.

story: The model for container orchestration was Google’s internal cluster manager, Borg. Instead of assigning services to particular machines, engineers described jobs and Borg decided where they ran, restarted them when they failed and packed different workloads onto shared machines to keep utilisation high. Its 2015 paper describes it running “hundreds of thousands of jobs” across clusters “each with up to tens of thousands of machines”, and summarises a decade of lessons.

Outside Google, the same idea emerged in research. Mesos, started at UC Berkeley by Benjamin Hindman, Andy Konwinski, Matei Zaharia and Ion Stoica and first presented in 2009, let several frameworks share one cluster; by 2010 Twitter was testing it. When Docker made the container image the standard unit of deployment in 2013, many companies wanted a Borg of their own. Google released Kubernetes in 2014, built on Borg’s lessons; Docker started Swarm the same year, and HashiCorp’s Nomad followed in 2015.

Kubernetes became the common choice: Microsoft and AWS announced managed Kubernetes services in 2017, and Apache retired Mesos to its Attic in 2025. Many teams now use it through managed Kubernetes or serverless container services that hide the cluster entirely.

choices.choice: Declare the goal, not the steps
choices.why: You state how many copies should run and the orchestrator keeps working toward it. Because controllers react to the current state rather than individual events, crashes and lost messages are corrected on the next pass instead of needing a script for every failure.

choices.choice: Pack mixed workloads onto shared machines
choices.why: Machines dedicated to one service often sit largely idle. Borg got its utilisation from placing many jobs per machine, over-committing resources and isolating performance, and Kubernetes schedules by CPU and memory requests for the same reason.

choices.choice: Give moving workloads a stable address
choices.why: If any container can be rescheduled anywhere, clients can’t track machines. Kubernetes separated naming, discovery and load balancing from the apps themselves, so a Service keeps one address while its Pods come and go.

timeline.text: Mesos first presented by UC Berkeley researchers
Google open-sources Kubernetes; Docker starts Swarm
Kubernetes 1.0, HashiCorp Nomad and the Borg paper all appear
Microsoft (AKS) and AWS (EKS) announce managed Kubernetes
Apache Mesos retired and moved to the Apache Attic
